reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a cryptocurrency arbitrage bot using unusually large reported returns, including an increase from 1.89 ETH to 23.621 ETH over 28 days. The demonstration links those claims to configuring a wallet address and private key, selecting a network, and allowing a maximum spend of 0.5 ETH. The speaker presents the content as a positive review, although the records do not establish that the displayed balances or profits were genuine or that funds or credentials were misused.

citations.quote: Hi everyone, this is my review on the Triangular Arbitrage.
this bot has really helped me and I hope it helps others
once you download the zip file and the link above the github link above in the description unzip it to a location
I ran it for 28 days straight and these are my results
that was from the utilization of just the 0.5

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present the reported result as a guaranteed outcome. The description puts use at the viewer's own risk, and the speaker expressly declines to vouch for the two networks he has not tested. He also distinguishes an estimated profit from what he says the bot produced. Those qualifications matter: this is a discussion of a tool and a personal test, not an assurance that viewers will reproduce the result.

citations.quote: disclaimer I'm no way of financial advisor use anything and any advice I give at your own risk.
I have not tested either one of those so I cannot give you feedback on those
estimated profit after fees that's what estimated

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited 28-day claim is a report of the speaker's own results, not a promise of the same result to every viewer. His review also describes a 0.5 maximum spend and explicitly limits his feedback on untested networks. The opening has reason to question whether the reported balance is verified, but lack of independent verification does not, by itself, establish that the speaker is offering a guaranteed return.

citations.quote: I ran it for 28 days straight and these are my results
for the max spend this is where I kept the default the default is 0.5 and I didn't change that
I have not tested either one of those so I cannot give you feedback on those

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A risk disclaimer and a caveat about other networks do not undo the video's central pitch. The speaker attributes a striking return to running this bot for 28 days, directs viewers to the download, and walks through entering a private key. The defense's quotes show qualifications, but they do not verify the returns or remove the risk created by encouraging viewers to configure wallet credentials for the promoted bot.

opening.argument: Judge, the video's sustained focus is an operational walkthrough. The speaker says how to open the configuration file, explains the maximum-spend setting, launches the local HTML file in a browser, and stops the bot to inspect its output. The sampled views show the configuration file and browser interface. The result claim supplies context for why he tried the software, but the material the viewer is actually taken through is how the tool is configured and run.

citations.quote: To configure it, you go to config.js. You're going to right click on that and go to edit
for the max spend this is where I kept the default the default is 0.5
I'm going to go down to index.html. I'm going to right click on that.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the reported result and the configuration steps as proof of a deceptive solicitation. But those same steps are the substance of a software demonstration: the speaker opens a local HTML file, runs the interface, then stops it to examine what appeared. The evidence does not establish that the displayed output is genuine, yet neither does it show a completed transfer or misuse of the wallet.

citations.quote: you basically can open with any kind of web browser you have
I'm going to stop the bot. We're going to look at this.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A walkthrough can also promote a risky return claim. Here the instruction is tied directly to the speaker's claimed 28-day result and favorable endorsement. Crucially, the walkthrough tells viewers to put a private key into the configuration file. The defense's local-file and interface evidence describes the presentation, but it does not establish that the bot is trustworthy or that the reported profits occurred.

this bot has really helped me and I hope it helps others

opening.argument: Judge, the offered item is described as free, open-source JavaScript available through a GitHub download. The demonstration shows files on the speaker's desktop and an interface opened from a local file. That does not certify the code as safe, but the supplied material shows no payment demand, deposit address for a promoter, or referral-income structure. The private-key entry is a serious reason to scrutinize the software; the record does not show that the key is sent to anyone or that funds are taken.

citations.quote: open source/free on GitHub
It is written in pure JavaScript easy to read ,easy to run and easy to modify if you wish to do so.
I unzipped it in my desktop
I input in my public address and private key and saved the config.js file.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies a wallet-key instruction and an unverified return claim. It does not identify a recipient for the key, an observed withdrawal, or evidence that the download costs money. The speaker describes the bot as open source and demonstrates it through local files. Those facts cannot prove safety, but they leave an important gap between a concerning product review and a demonstrated credential-theft or deposit scheme.

citations.quote: it's open source freely available on github
I input in my public address and private key and saved the config.js file.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The concern is not limited to a proven theft or paid download. This video promotes a bot through an extraordinary displayed increase over 28 days, provides a download link, and instructs viewers to configure it with a private key and spending limit. Free or locally opened software can still expose funds. The defense's evidence does not establish what the code does with credentials, and the claimed returns remain unverified.
